Thanks for engaging, Balaji. 

The DoorDash point is a continuation of a theme I've been writing about for a while (in my Deep Dives and, more recently, on autonomous delivery), which is probably why I didn't spell it out again here. I intended it to be a narrower claim than you may have interpreted. Yes, DoorDash's international footprint was largely bought. My point is about new verticals at home, where DoorDash has shown a greater willingness to build while Uber has tended to buy.

On 2022-24, you're obviously right that Uber didn't deploy much in that window. But it deployed a good chunk on either side of it: Careem, Postmates, Drizly, Cornershop and Transplace before, and SpotHero, Getir, Delivery Hero and now ezCater after. Uber's own capital allocation framework earmarks roughly half of FCF for uses other than capital return, so I assumed that pattern may continue rather than 2022-24 to be the norm.

On ezCater, I take the point that order size matters. But the larger tickets allegedly come with half the commission, and we don't know the exact take rate. The press release said the business is profitable on a non-GAAP basis, which presumably means it isn't on a GAAP basis. There may well be meaningful synergies, and it may be accretive on a margin basis once restructuring costs are excluded. The release just didn't give much clarity on such synergy or the margin profile.

Finally, I'm certainly not suggesting Uber is Expedia. Uber's 2022-25 bottom line CAGR likely reflects a low starting base too. More importantly, the point I was really trying to land is simpler: it's not easy for investors to judge a bunch of acquisitions and underwrite a return profile on that capital. Organic reinvestment is relatively easier to underwrite; with M&A, you need a separate view on every deal, and the answers may take years to emerge. I'm not claiming these are destined to be bad investments... just that they're harder to underwrite, and the outcome of such capital allocation will matter a LOT for long-term shareholders in terms of whether the stock compounds at an attractive rate over the next 5-10 years.
